claims.text: A laser-clad refractory high-entropy alloy coating can be applied to stainless steel.
The laser-clad coating significantly improves the corrosion resistance of stainless steel.
The improvement results from formation of a dense, Cr-enhanced passive surface film.
Conventional stainless steel has suboptimal corrosion resistance in aggressive environments such as 3.5 wt% NaCl.
WVTaTiCr-based refractory high-entropy alloy coatings with varied Cr content can be deposited by laser cladding.
The proposed coating is deposited on stainless steel.
Corrosion behavior is evaluated in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution.
The corrosion tests are conducted at room temperature.
Laser cladding produces a refined coating microstructure that promotes precipitation of a Cr-rich Cr2Ta Laves phase.
The coating develops a dense passive layer containing Cr and Ti oxides.
Laser cladding creates a metallurgically bonded coating with a fine dendritic structure.
Added Cr promotes lattice distortion.
Added Cr drives formation of protective intermetallic phases and oxides.
The protective phases and oxides impede ion diffusion and reduce active corrosion relative to bare stainless steel.
The coated stainless steel will have a higher corrosion potential than uncoated stainless steel.
The coated stainless steel will have lower corrosion current density and corrosion rate than uncoated stainless steel.
Uncoated stainless steel exhibits relatively high corrosion current density and extensive attack in chloride-containing environments.
Performance under extreme thermal or mechanical stress remains unvalidated.
The magnitude and durability of the corrosion benefit may depend on coating composition, processing parameters, and environment.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant reduction of at least 50% in both corrosion current density and weight loss relative to an uncoated control falsifies the hypothesis.
